passages.text: When dawn came, our father went in with our mother and the three sons to where Peter was. He greeted him and sat down; then we too sat down at Peter's bidding. Looking directly at our father, Peter said, ‘I am eager for you to become of one mind with your wife and children, so that you may share their way of life here and, there too, after the soul's separation from the body, be with them free from sorrow. Or does not your being apart from one another cause the greatest distress to both you and them?’ Our father answered, ‘Very much indeed.’ Peter said, ‘If being separated from one another distresses you even here, since after death you are certainly bound not to be together, will it not distress you much more—you, a wise man, being separated from your family because of your opinion, and them suffering still more in knowing that eternal punishment awaits you for thinking otherwise, by the pronouncement of an explicit decree?’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁμόφρονά σε γενέσθαι γυναικὶ καὶ τέκνοις
lexical_decisions.chosen: you to become of one mind with your wife and children
lexical_decisions.rationale: The desired agreement concerns their beliefs in the ensuing discussion; it is not reduced to living at the same address or expanded into agreement on every possible matter.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ θάνατον πάντως ὀφειλόμενον ὑμῖν μετ’ ἀλλήλων μὴ εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: since after death you are certainly bound not to be together
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause states the anticipated separation emphatically within Peter's warning. Its connection to the father's different beliefs is supplied by the surrounding explicit clauses, not by removing the source's certainty.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by the pronouncement of an explicit decree
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive adjective can mean expressly stated or definite. Decree or ordinance preserves the authoritative ruling; the source does not identify a particular quoted verse or name its speaker here.

passages.text: Our father said, ‘But, dearest friend, souls are not punished in Hades, since the soul dissolves into air as soon as it leaves the body.’ Peter said, ‘Until we persuade you about this, then, answer me: does it not seem to you that, while you do not suffer distress because you disbelieve in punishment, they, being convinced of it, must be troubled about you?’ Our father said, ‘Your argument follows.’ Peter said, ‘Why, then, will you not relieve them of their very great sorrow about you by agreeing with our worship? I do not mean from embarrassment, but from good judgment, listening to what I tell you and judging whether it is so or not. If things are as we say, you will share enjoyment with your dearest ones here and share their rest there. But if, in examining your arguments, you show that what we say is a false myth, you will do well even so: having brought them to your own way of thinking, you will stop them from relying on empty hopes and free them from false fears.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ θρησκείᾳ συνθέμενος, οὐ δυσωπίᾳ λέγω, ἀλλ’ εὐγνωμοσύνῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: by agreeing with our worship? I do not mean from embarrassment, but from good judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: Θρησκεία concerns religious observance or worship; our is inferred from Peter's invitation. Δυσωπία can denote shamefaced compliance or reluctance to disappoint, contrasted with sound judgment rather than mere social acquiescence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν τῇ τῶν λόγων σου σκέψει
lexical_decisions.rationale: The possessive your is retained rather than silently changed to our. The father's own examination or examination of his arguments can both be heard in the genitive construction.

The future middle addresses the father and continues the togetherness expressed by the preceding compound. Rest is retained without adding a location or detailed doctrine of the afterlife not given here.

passages.text: Our father said, ‘You seem to me to be saying many reasonable things.’ Peter said, ‘Tell me, then, what is holding you back from coming to our faith, so that we may begin to speak directly to it. There are many things that hold people back. For those already convinced, there are the demands of purchases, business, farming, anxieties, and things of that sort. For unbelievers, among whom you too belong, there are assumptions: thinking that gods who do not exist do exist, or that everything is subject to birth-fate or to chance, or that souls are mortal, or that our message is false because there is no providence.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: Genesis here can denote the determining configuration or fate associated with birth, as distinguished from chance in the next alternative. Birth-fate keeps the birth wording visible; fate determined by the stars at birth is a fuller contextual alternative, but stars are not expressly named in this clause.
The noun refers to spontaneous occurrence without directing providence. It is not rendered automation, a misleading modern technical association.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the demands of purchases, business, farming, anxieties
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural occupations or lack of leisure is the governing idea, and all four listed sources of preoccupation are retained.

passages.text: ‘But I say that everything is governed by God's providence, judging from what has happened to you: your separation from your family for so many years. Since, if they had remained with you, perhaps they would not have listened to the teachings of reverence for God, their journey abroad with their mother was arranged, along with shipwreck, presumed death, and loss of contact. So too was their education in Greek and godless doctrines, so that, knowing them, they might be better able to refute them. After this came their love for the teaching of reverence for God and their ability to join me in helping my proclamation; then their brother Clement's coming together with us, and thus their mother's being recognized and becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing. Shortly afterward came the twins' being recognized and recognizing in turn, and, on the following day, meeting you and your recovering your family. I do not think that so swift a harmony, converging from every direction upon one intended aim, is without providence.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ναυφραγίῳ καὶ θανάτου ὑπονοίᾳ καὶ ἀπαρτίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: along with shipwreck, presumed death, and loss of contact
lexical_decisions.rationale: The list describes the circumstances of the family separation. Ἀπαρτία is read as absence of news or contact in this context; the translation does not supply a particular duration beyond the previously stated years.

lexical_decisions.chosen: becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The mother continues as the inferred person receiving assurance. Θεότης is divinity or divine nature, whose precise referent the clause leaves unnamed; this is not translated as an assertion that the mother herself became divine or that Peter was a god.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δίδυμα τέκνα ἐπιγνωσθέντα καὶ ἐπιγνόντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the twins' being recognized and recognizing in turn
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both passive and active recognition are retained. The unexpressed object of their recognition is not replaced by an invented named person in this clause.

The convergence is toward one aim of intention or purpose. Agreement of belief is a possible contextual emphasis for γνώμη, but the preceding arrangement of events favors an intended aim without naming a separate planner in this phrase.

passages.text: Our father began to say to Peter, ‘Do not suppose, my dearest Peter, that I have not been thinking about the message you proclaim. Indeed, at the end of this past night, when Clement urged me at length to agree with the truth you proclaim, I answered, “What newer instruction can anyone give beyond what the ancients advised?” He smiled gently and said, “There is a great difference, father, between the teachings of reverence for God and those of philosophy. For the message of truth has its proof from prophecy, whereas the teaching of philosophy offers fine language and seems to present its proofs from conjectures.” Having said this, however, he set out for me, as an example, the teaching about love for humanity that you had explained to him. It seemed to me, rather, utterly unjust. I will tell you how. He said that it was just for someone to offer the other cheek as well to the person striking his cheek; to give his head-covering too to the person taking his cloak; to go two miles with the person compelling him to go one; and other things of this sort.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καλλιλογίας παρέχων ἐκ στοχασμῶν δοκεῖ παριστᾶν τὰς ἀποδείξεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the teaching of philosophy offers fine language and seems to present its proofs from conjectures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The favorable-sounding language and the qualification seems are retained alongside the criticism of conjectural proofs. The translation does not replace conjecture by observation or prophecy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν περὶ φιλανθρωπίας μοι ἐξέθετο λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he set out for me ... the teaching about love for humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term is a broad humane love or kindness toward human beings. Love for humanity keeps its human object explicit and connects it with the ensuing discussion of humane treatment.
The garment can be a scarf, kerchief, or head-covering. It is distinguished from the cloak named immediately before it, rather than replaced by the tunic familiar from another form of the saying.
